paper.title: Learning Game-Playing Agents with Generative Code Optimization
paper.central_claim: Policies written as modular Python programs and refined by an LLM generative optimizer (Trace/OptoPrime) from execution traces and tiered natural-language feedback reach performance competitive with DQN/PPO on Pong, Breakout and Space Invaders with far less wall-clock training time and fewer environment interactions.

evidence.quote: We present a generative optimization approach for learning game-playing agents, where policies are represented as Python programs and refined using large language models (LLMs).
evidence.support_explanation: Central claim: policy code is the optimized object.

evidence.quote: Applied to Atari games, our game-playing Python program achieves performance competitive with deep reinforcement learning (RL) baselines while using significantly less training time and much fewer environment interactions.
evidence.support_explanation: Headline efficiency/competitiveness claim.

evidence.quote: Our approach departs from prior work by: (i) treating the policy code itself as the object of optimization, (ii) extracting rich execution traces to localize failure points, and (iii) prompting an LLM iteratively with graph-based backtracing to propose meaningful code updates.
evidence.support_explanation: Authors' differentiation; (ii)-(iii) are inherited from Trace.

evidence.quote: A key difference from prior work is the complexity of our domain: while Trace focuses on short-horizon tasks (e.g. Meta-World environments with at most 10 decision steps), Atari games require hundreds and thousands of steps per episode with sparse rewards, introducing longer temporal dependencies and credit assignment challenges.
evidence.support_explanation: The residual claimed: Trace was only shown on short-horizon tasks.

evidence.quote: We train agents in an episodic reinforcement learning setup, where each iteration consists of a single rollout.
evidence.support_explanation: One short rollout per optimisation iteration.

signatures.object: Trainable Python functions of a hand-structured policy (predict_ball_trajectory/select_action etc.; decide_shoot/decide_movement)
signatures.information: Object-centric observations (OCAtari positions/velocities), reward, traced execution graph of the rollout, tiered NL feedback derived from a ~4000-step evaluation episode; docstrings with game constants
signatures.operation: OptoPrime (LLM, Claude-3.5-Sonnet) backward pass over the traced graph with feedback, then step() rewrites the trainable code (20 iterations, optimizer memory 5)
signatures.output: New policy code; best iterate retained for reporting
signatures.conditions: rollout caps 400/300/15 steps by context window; user supplies interfaces, docstrings, starter code, feedback schedule
signatures.feedback: Trace graph of the short rollout + reward level of a long evaluation episode mapped to hand-written advice
signatures.selection_rule: Not described for acceptance of edits; best iteration reported (Table 4 'Best')
signatures.selection_data: the same environment/evaluation episode that supplies feedback
signatures.persistence: the Python policy file; last 5 updates in optimizer context
signatures.claimed_effect: Pong 21, Breakout 353, Space Invaders 1200 in 43/91/36 min
signatures.failure_boundary: unstable edits, context-window limited horizon, plateaus with reward-only feedback

gap.author_gap: Deep RL needs millions of interactions and yields opaque policies; programmatic policies are hard to optimise; LLM code optimisation for agent policies in long-horizon Atari is unexplored.
gap.checked_gap: Sample-inefficiency/opacity is a real general limitation, but the specific gap is 'Trace has only been shown on <=10-step tasks' - largely a domain-application gap. The paper does not show a failure of prior LLM-in-the-loop code/policy evolution on Atari.

G.reason: Opus sides with son55. The paper's gap is a first application of an existing optimizer to a new domain (opus:O06); Trace's short horizon is untested scope, not a located failure (opus:O07); the closest LLM code-policy optimisers (LangProp) and programmatic-policy lineage are listed, not compared; the domain card names this failure shape (H09 parent F1/F3: game-player deliverable as the vehicle).
